newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia struggles to enforce logging ban.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia struggles to enforce logging ban.

text.p: Cambodia's top forestry official on Monday declared a new ban on log exports a success but conceded the government does not have full control over the country's dwindling forests.

"Ninety-nine percent of the country supports this ban, but there are still some illegal loggers," said Agriculture Minister Tao Seng Huor at a news conference. He noted that some logging may be continuing in areas held by former Khmer Rouge rebels.
"The government will not be able to get any of that money," he noted.
Logging was one of the most explosive issues in Cambodia last year.

The International Monetary Fund cancelled a $20 million loan to Cambodia in November last year after it became increasingly frustrated with what it called a lack of transparency in the government's forestry policy and accounting for logging revenues.

Heavy logging and massive forestry concessions raised an outcry from international watchdog groups and some Cambodian politicians, who signed a petition protesting the government's lack of resolve in addressing the problem.

Cambodia, once one of the most heavily forested countries in the world, has lost more than three million hectares (7.4 million acres) of forest in the past three decades, according to the World Bank and United Nations.

In the face of mounting pressure, the government announced a December 31 ban on log exports and vowed to take strong measures to enforce the rule, including hiring a Swiss company to monitor the country's borders.
But representatives of that firm, Societe Generale de Surveillance (SGS), are not due to arrive in Cambodia for another week.
Tao Seng Huor acknowledged he had heard reports of Thai companies securing a 600 million baht ($23 million) deal to export logs from former Khmer Rouge guerrillas in the northwest base of Samlaut.
Nonetheless, the minister told reporters he expected the government would gain control of the situation soon, allowing it to someday conduct "environmentally sound" logging.
"When we have stability, we can lift the ban," he said.
